other_material_facts.label: industry_evidence
other_material_facts.value: According to the World Bank, global manufacturing Gross Value Added (“GVA”) to global economy reached ₹1,430.12 trillion (US$16.82 trillion) in Calendar Year (“CY”) 2024, up from ₹1,156.45 trillion (US$13.61 trillion) in CY2020 growing at a Compound Annual Growth Rate (“CAGR”) of 5.45%.

other_material_facts.label: industry_evidence
other_material_facts.value: Between CY2014 and CY2022, China’s manufacturing GVA increased from ₹270.66 trillion (US$3.18 trillion) to ₹411.40 trillion (US$4.84 trillion), reflecting a CAGR of 5.37%.

other_material_facts.label: industry_evidence
other_material_facts.value: However, over CY2022 to CY2024, its manufacturing GVA declined at a CAGR of 1.86%, indicating a moderation in growth momentum and gradual adjustment in its share of global manufacturing output.

other_material_facts.label: industry_evidence
other_material_facts.value: Structural growth drivers are sustaining manufacturing expansion in India and the United States Among the economies positioned to benefit from this realignment, India and the United States represent two distinct but complementary manufacturing trajectories - India driven by rapid capacity addition, localization, and rising domestic demand, and the US by policy-led re-industrialization, reshoring, and technology modernization.

other_material_facts.label: industry_evidence
other_material_facts.value: As of CY2024, India’s manufacturing GVA stood at ₹41.68 trillion (US$490.40 billion), compared to ₹26.11 trillion (US$307.21 billion) in CY2014, reflecting a CAGR of approximately 4.79% over the period.

other_material_facts.label: industry_evidence
other_material_facts.value: During the same timeframe, global manufacturing GVA grew at a CAGR of approximately 2.86%, indicating a comparatively higher growth rate (~1.7 times) for India relative to the global average.

other_material_facts.label: industry_evidence
other_material_facts.value: India’s ongoing manufacturing upcycle is being sustained by three structural growth drivers.

other_material_facts.label: industry_evidence
other_material_facts.value: Thermal power installed capacity in India expanded at a CAGR of ~1% between FY2021 and FY2026, growing from 234.73 GW in FY2021 to 249.27 GW in FY2026 and estimated to grow further to 315.91 GW in FY2033.

overview.business_overview:
We are a technology-led, asset-light manufacturing platform for industrial and consumer goods in India and globally. We aggregate manufacturing capacity across a network of third-party suppliers and our own facilities into a “universal factory,” unified through Zetwerk OS, our proprietary technology backbone. Our customers range across sizes, from innovative startups to mature companies, and across industries, including utilities, renewables, consumer electronics, artificial intelligence infrastructure, aerospace, space & defence, oil & gas, and industrial automation. Some of our customers include Siemens Gamesa, Acer India Private Limited, boAt, NextPower (formerly Nextracker), CG Power and Industrial Solutions Limited, NTPC Renewable Energy Limited, L&T MHI Power Boiler Pvt Ltd, DRDO (Electronics & Radar Development Establishment (LRDE)), National Aluminium Company Limited, Indian Oil Corporation Limited, Mortenson, Nordex Acciona, Indian Air Force, and Numaligarh Refinery Limited. Third-party suppliers with whom we work have capabilities in manufacturing processes, including sheet metal stamping, metal fabrication, injection moulding, extrusions, assembly, die casting, forging, grinding and machining, and span several countries, including industrial geographies such as India, Vietnam, Thailand, Taiwan, Germany, Spain, Eastern Europe, Mexico and the USA. Since our incorporation, we have cumulatively delivered products and raw materials worth ₹743,742.10 million in terms of GMV to our customers.

According to the Redseer Report: manufacturing capacity is often globally fragmented, with production typically carried out in uncoordinated, discrete facilities characterised by variable quality and inconsistent service levels, making scaling inefficient and unreliable. This challenge is particularly pronounced in new, high-growth industries such as renewable energy, artificial intelligence, defense, aerospace, and space exploration, where rapid growth in demand for manufactured goods is often bottlenecked by supply chain constraints. For instance, industry average lead times for power transformer manufacturing range from 30-36 months in India to 36-42 months in the United States.

We are well positioned to address these challenges and pursue manufacturing opportunities in new industries. We enable our customers to build complex products faster, across multiple geographies, while meeting quality requirements and maintaining competitive costs. Our platform model is designed to scale capacity and capabilities in an asset‑light manner. We are focused on accelerating time to market for our customers. By aggregating spare capacity from multiple third‑party suppliers, we are able to manufacture products at low cost while optimising for speed and quality. Zetwerk OS, our proprietary technology, drives the end‑to‑end order flow, from supplier selection and digital recipes to project management, quality control, and logistics. Our manufacturing platform can distribute a single order across multiple third‑party suppliers and our own manufacturing facilities, enabling simultaneous manufacturing. Through such distribution, we are also able to break geographic barriers, enabling us to serve customers using suppliers across geographies. Through a combination of the capabilities mentioned above and the inherent benefits of a platform model, we have been able to build a large base of customers.

Our Journey: The Evolution of Our Manufacturing Platform Our Company was incorporated in December 2017. Our Promoters, Amrit Pratik Acharya and Srinath Ramakkrushnan, bring experience in manufacturing sourcing from their previous professional roles at ITC.

In our early stages, we operated as a pure manufacturing marketplace, with demand sourced entirely from India and supplied exclusively through Indian suppliers. Our initial focus was on aggregating suppliers for capital goods products that were typically project‑based and non‑recurring in nature. For example, customers setting up greenfield manufacturing facilities would engage us to source machinery or machine components. Such orders were generally one‑time, with limited follow‑on requirements other than spare parts.

Over time, we intentionally diversified the platform across multiple growth vectors, including:

• adding design‑led capabilities by offering original design manufacturing (“ODM”) solutions for select customers and components;

• expanding our supplier base internationally and also to include a broader range of manufacturing processes capable

• selectively establishing our own manufacturing facilities.

As a result, we have evolved from an India‑only marketplace catering to limited industries into a diversified and resilient manufacturing platform with multiple demand engines, a multi-geography supplier base and an expanded capability for customers in India and internationally.

Growth of our Recurring Components Business

According to the Redseer Report, capital expenditure is largely project-based, with demand being non-recurring in nature and closely linked to macroeconomic cycles.  The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the cyclical nature of this project-driven operating model, prompting us to diversify from our original focus on one-time “capex”-related products to also serving original equipment manufacturers (“OEMs”) with recurring components linked to their ongoing opex budgets, such as torque tubes for NextPower, laptops and motherboards for Acer India Private Limited and transformer lamination for companies such as Bharat Bijlee Ltd. We believe this diversification from predominantly one-time capex products to a mix of capex products and recurring components has made our revenue more predictable, enabling us to keep growing even when capex-related demand was lower, as was the case in Fiscal 2025. International Business Expansion

According to the Redseer Report, global manufacturing is entering a new phase of re-industrialisation and strategic rebalancing. While earlier industrial cycles were driven by export competitiveness and deep global integration, the current decade is defined by resilience, supply security, and geographic diversification. Governments across major economies are advancing industrial policy to strengthen domestic manufacturing bases, while companies are expanding production footprints beyond traditional hubs to mitigate concentration risk. Countries such as India are actively positioning themselves as alternative manufacturing destinations, attracting investment as firms seek to build more distributed and resilient supply chains.

We began focused expansion outside India in Fiscal 2022 and have since added customers in the USA and Europe and suppliers in Vietnam, Mexico and the USA. Manufacturing Business revenue from international markets was ₹6,783.72 million and ₹6,017.96 million for the three months periods ended June 30, 2026 and June 30, 2025 respectively and ₹27,753.55 million, ₹23,334.89 million and ₹28,327.77 million for Fiscal 2026, Fiscal 2025 and Fiscal 2024, respectively. In addition, as some of our customers have grown into large accounts, we have selectively invested in our own assembly and finishing facilities to serve them, evolving from a pure marketplace to a hybrid model that combines manufacturing and assembly both through third parties and our own manufacturing facilities. We have also added in-house engineering and design capabilities for certain components, including those used for transformers for AI data centres, process plant machinery, metal manufacturing and defence applications. Our operations span design, manufacturing, quality control, logistics, customs, documentation and compliance, all coordinated through our proprietary Zetwerk OS. We serve both Indian and international customers and offer them the ability to source both one-time capital goods for capex projects as well as recurring components that form part of their opex. Our value propositions, detailed below, foster customer loyalty, with high rates of repeat customers, growing customer spending with us and an expanding range of products manufactured through our manufacturing platform. We have built long-term relationships with some customers through multi-year, take-or-pay contracts, providing revenue visibility and recurring business. In Fiscal 2026, our top 10 customers (based on their contribution to Revenue from Manufacturing Business) have been with us for an average of 2.8 years, out of the approximately eight years since we commenced operations. Our customer retention is reflected in our Fiscal 2023 to Fiscal 2026 median Manufacturing Business Net Revenue Retention (“NRR”) of 128.85% (NRR stood at 175.49% in Fiscal 2023, 137.46% in Fiscal 2024, 87.13% in Fiscal 2025 and 120.24% in Fiscal 2026). Our key value propositions to customers are:

• Time to market: We accelerate our customers’ time to market by enabling simultaneous manufacturing by splitting the execution of an order across multiple qualified suppliers. On average, an order was allocated to 7 suppliers in Fiscal 2026, as compared to 6 suppliers in Fiscal 2025 and 3 in Fiscal 2024, significantly reducing manufacturing timelines. Our upfront investment in engineering, manufacturability analysis and design readiness minimises iterations and shortens production cycles, while our technology platform automates workflow to eliminate manual process delays. For example, our committed delivery timelines for supplying power transformers to the USA in Fiscal 2026 were 12 to 15 months. According to the Redseer Report, industry average lead times for power transformer manufacturing range from 30-36 months in India to 36-42 months in the United States, reflecting the extended procurement cycles associated with energy infrastructure expansion in both markets.  This contributed to customers placing orders worth ₹20,322.52 million for power transformers in Fiscal 2026.

• Quality assurance: Our manufacturing platform is designed to consistently meet customer‑defined quality requirements across orders. As our manufacturing platform scales, quality improves through better data, process controls, enhanced review processes, follow-up discipline, and proactive communication with partners. We apply a stringent screening process before onboarding suppliers and conduct regular checks through our technology-led monitoring programme to ensure consistent quality, removing suppliers that fail to meet our standards. Our supplier onboarding and verification process is governed by a standard operating procedure and includes comprehensive KYC documentation verification, validation of MSME certificates, where applicable, and independent cross‑verification of goods and services tax details on the relevant government portal to confirm authenticity, and registered particulars. We also verify supplier bank accounts through ‘penny tests’ to confirm the accuracy of account details and mitigate payment‑related risks.

All submissions are subject to manual review, and any discrepancies identified must be resolved prior to onboarding. Following onboarding, system‑level controls are implemented to restrict deletion of vendor records and modification of critical KYC information, thereby ensuring ongoing data integrity and compliance. For example, we delivered washing machine controllers to a precision electronics customer with a defect rate of 200 ppm. According to the Redseer Report, a typical quality benchmark for components such as washing machine controllers is 500 ppm.

• Cost-effective manufacturing: We deliver cost-efficient manufacturing by unlocking underutilised capacity at competitive prices across our global supplier network. For instance, we fulfilled a public sector undertaking tender, where we are required to be L1 (lowest cost) to win the tender, by leveraging the manufacturing capacities of suppliers within our network. Our technology-led approach identifies optimal prices based on our parameters for each order within our network and allocates production accordingly. We also actively locate and identify suppliers with structural tariff advantage depending on their location and add them to our platform. For instance, in 2025, we onboarded transformer suppliers in Oman who were subject to a 10% tariff on exports to the USA, compared to Indian suppliers who faced a 50% tariff at the time, which enabled us to lower our cost to supply transformers to USA customers. Our scale also enables suppliers to source raw materials at lower costs, further enhancing cost-effectiveness. Our ability to provide competitively priced products is a key driver of repeat orders on our manufacturing platform. Our customer retention is reflected in our Fiscal 2023 to Fiscal 2026 median NRR of 128.85% (NRR stood at 175.49% in Fiscal 2023, 137.46% in Fiscal 2024, 87.13% in Fiscal 2025 and 120.24% in Fiscal 2026). Revenue from Repeat Customers in our Manufacturing Business was 89.26% for the three months period ended June 30, 2026, 95.36% for the three months period ended June 30, 2025, 80.15% in Fiscal 2026, 84.80% in Fiscal 2025 and 78.11% in Fiscal 2024.

• Breadth of sourcing: We serve as a “one-stop shop” for customers looking to purchase multiple products across categories. This allows customers to move from single‑product sourcing to multi‑category programmes. For instance, we supplied power transformers to a renewable energy customer in the USA and subsequently broadened the relationship to include solar components. Similarly, for one of the solar customers in the USA, we initially supplied assemblies before expanding to provide torque tubes. In Precision Products, we began our relationship with Acer India Private Limited by providing them with motherboards and personal laptops before expanding into components, televisions and interactive flat panel displays.

• Ability to scale supply to demand: By aggregating multiple suppliers and manufacturing facilities, we provide customers with access to the full range of production volumes, from small runs to large-scale mass production. This enables customers to absorb rapid growth in demand and accelerate new product innovation and launch cycles. For example, our sales of torque tubes for NextPower increased from US$39.14 million in Fiscal 2024 to US$78.70 million in Fiscal 2026.

• End-to-end services: According to the Redseer Report, OEMs today face greater complexity in managing cross-border multi-party supply chains and coordinating multiple suppliers’ pricing, timing and inconsistent quality.  Thus, our ability to offer a transparent, seamless experience across the entire manufacturing lifecycle, including design, manufacturing, quality control, logistics, customs, documentation and compliance, is a key value proposition for our customers. This frees customers from the time, complexity and cost of coordinating with multiple partners. For example, we executed a 1.5 GW module supply order for NTPC Renewable Energy Limited, coordinating with more than six manufacturers, 25 transporters and multiple third-party quality inspectors, among others. We also provide customers with access to our in-house design and development capabilities, working with them to co-create, prototype and innovate new products. Manufacturing Business Share of GMV from ODM Contracts was 13.66% and 6.78% for the three months periods ended June 30, 2026 and June 30, 2025, respectively, and grew from 8.12% in Fiscal 2024 to 13.93% in Fiscal 2026.

Our Supplier Base

In Fiscal 2026, our supplier base comprised 6,979 third-party suppliers across 26 countries, including India, and our 26 manufacturing facilities across four countries, including India. Our third-party supplier base includes SMEs and specialised manufacturers with advanced capabilities in casting, machining, fabrication, moulding, surface treatment, and other specialised operations. According to the Redseer Report, as of Fiscal 2026, our manufacturing process capabilities are diverse and extensive compared to SME manufacturers, which typically have 2 to 5 manufacturing process capabilities. We invest in long-term relationships with our suppliers, providing the tools, guidance on audit procedures and other requirements, and support their need to meet our customers’ quality and delivery standards.

Our value proposition to suppliers includes:

• Revenue predictability and improved capacity utilisation: We provide our suppliers with demand visibility, which we believe enables them to optimise manufacturing asset utilisation and increase revenue. Traditional manufacturing companies typically operate within specific product segments or end-use industries, with their financial profile shaped by the capital intensity, margin structure, and demand cyclicality of that segment, according to the Redseer Report. We help our suppliers access demand from additional verticals by giving them orders that use their existing assets for products they may not typically make. Through our global manufacturing platform, we also enable our suppliers to access demand across geographies. For example, in Fiscal 2021, to meet demand for solar platforms in the USA, we enabled KL Steel to execute one of our customer orders.

• Front-loaded engineering and design enablement: For certain products, we perform in-house ODM engineering and design validation of customer specifications-including, for example, for transformer manufacturing in the USA. These validations improve manufacturing efficiency for our suppliers by reducing iterations and enabling faster production. We achieved a first pass rate of approximately 99% (calculated by dividing the number of orders completed correctly on the first attempt, without rework or iterations after the supplier completed its work, by the total number of orders, multiplied by 100%) on all orders completed by third-party suppliers in Fiscal 2026. Manufacturing Business share of GMV from recurring components grew from 49.85% in Fiscal 2024 to 50.85% in Fiscal 2026, and from 58.34% in the three months period ended June 30, 2025 to 71.20% in the three months period ended June 30, 2026.

• Ability to source raw materials efficiently and cost-effectively: We provide our suppliers with access to raw materials at competitive prices and facilitate access to working capital and financing.

To complement our third-party supplier network, we have established in-house manufacturing capabilities through 26 facilities across four countries, including India, as of June 30, 2026. These facilities primarily provide assembly and finishing operations for parts and components sourced mainly from our third-party suppliers. We acquired these facilities through a combination of greenfield investments based on visible customer demand and acquisitions of operating facilities. These facilities enable us to enter select markets with high entry barriers and structural incentives for in-house manufacturing. For example, we receive incentives under the Indian government’s PLI Scheme and Electronic Component Manufacturing Scheme for manufacturing IT hardware such as laptops, tablets and servers, consumer electronics such as LED lights and air conditioner components, as well as multi-layer PCBs and optical transceivers-small form-factor pluggable. We are also able to execute large or complex orders that require a high degree of manufacturing control, expanding our ability to service orders that would not be possible under a distributed model. For certain large customers with multi-year orders, we manufacture through our own facilities often located near customer sites that ensure a high level of control over design, production and quality. Examples include our facility in Las Vegas, USA, which manufactures torque tubes for NextPower, and our facility in Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India, which manufactures washing machine components.
